outcome: Two post-window preprints settle further cases of Fröberg's conjecture on the Hilbert series of ideals generated by generic/general forms: Boij–Dannetun–Lundqvist (arXiv:2605.03872, May 2026) prove the conjecture in the second non-trivial degree for generic forms of degree d>2, and up to degree 2d-1 for sufficiently many variables; Wang–Zhang (arXiv:2608.24797, August 2026) prove it for general forms of degree 5 and 7 in four variables for every generator count r≥1, extending the previously known range (r≤5, and the equal-degree theorem through degree d+2). The general conjecture (arbitrary number of forms, degrees, and variables) remains open. Neither preprint has yet been digested by an expert (no journal publication, no blog/survey treatment found), so status is 'partial' rather than 'resolved' for either event.

ai.basis_quote: The main results of this paper were obtained through a generative-AI workflow using OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, Anthropic Claude Fable 5, and Grok 4.6. ... The AI-assisted workflow used [these systems] for the formulation of mathematical ideas, generation of conjectures and proof strategies, derivation and checking of intermediate steps, construction of examples and exact certificates, comparison of literature and candidate proof approaches, organization of arguments, LaTeX drafting, and revision of the final text.

summary: Fröberg's conjecture (Wikipedia's 2024 wording: on the Hilbert function/series of an ideal generated by a set of generic forms) has not been resolved in general, but two preprints since the frozen revision settle additional special cases, which is squarely within scope under §3.1 since both restrict the same stated question (fewer variables/degrees/generator counts) rather than changing it. (1) Boij, Dannetun and Lundqvist, 'Independence of generic forms and the Fröberg conjecture' (arXiv:2605.03872, submitted 2026-05-05), prove the conjecture in the second non-trivial degree for generic forms of any degree d>2, and up to degree 2d-1 when the number of variables is large enough — a genuine, human-authored extension of the known range, with no AI involvement found in the fetched text (ai_role: none for that paper). (2) Wang and Zhang, 'Fröberg's Conjecture for Quintics and Septics in Four Variables' (arXiv:2608.24797, v1 2026-08-25, v3 2026-08-27), prove the conjecture for r general forms of degree 5 or 7 in exactly four variables for every r≥1, closing the previously-open generator-count gaps (6≤r≤11 for quintics, 6≤r≤21 for septics) beyond the classical r≤5 case and Boij–Dannetun–Lundqvist's degree d+2 bound. This second paper is the one carrying the AI signal: its own acknowledgements state the results were 'obtained through a generative-AI workflow' using three named systems for 'formulation of mathematical ideas, generation of conjectures and proof strategies, derivation ... of intermediate steps, construction of examples and exact certificates,' i.e. AI systems producing mathematics that appears in the final result (constructions/certificates), not merely checking or formalising human work — this clears the 'assisted' bar under §6.2. It could also be read as 'generated' (the AI produced the proof strategy and the certificates, and the human role appears reducible to running/rebuilding verification scripts), but the authors' own framing is 'computer-assisted' work by named human authors with AI as a tool within a structured workflow, not 'the model produced the proof and we verified it,' so I coded 'assisted' and flag the alternative. The paper is an unrefereed preprint (v3, dated 2026-08-27, revising only the AI-disclosure and acknowledgements, not the theorem or proof) with no evidence of expert digestion, journal acceptance, or treatment on expert blogs (Tao's site was checked and has no mention). An independent third-party site (VibeMathed, which catalogs AI-involved math results) reports it re-derived the Macaulay-matrix computations from the paper's printed data and reproduced all ten quintic endpoint rows exactly, but explicitly notes 'the mathematical reduction to endpoints wasn't independently checked' and 'the paper is unrefereed with no human expert review' — so this counts as partial computational corroboration, not expert digestion, keeping status at 'partial' rather than 'resolved'. Neither result is a counterexample; both confirm the conjectured Hilbert series formula in the cases they cover, hence resolution_direction 'confirmed'. The Wikipedia article itself is unchanged since 2024 (still a stub with only the statement and two 1980s/1990s references), consistent with this being progress not yet reflected in secondary digestion.
competing_reading: The Wang–Zhang paper could be coded ai_role 'generated' rather than 'assisted': the acknowledgements credit the AI systems with generating 'proof strategies,' 'exact certificates,' and doing the actual derivation of intermediate steps, with the named human authors' visible contribution largely limited to running verification scripts and drafting/revision oversight — arguably 'the model produced the proof and the humans verified it' per §6.2's generated/assisted distinction. I coded 'assisted' because the authors describe a 'workflow' they directed and do not say a model single-handedly produced the mathematics with the humans only checking it; but with only the arXiv HTML available (no access to any interview or supplementary methods statement), the line is genuinely close.
what_would_settle_it: A supplementary methods statement, author interview, or version-history comment from Wang and Zhang clarifying the division of labor (did a human devise the reduction to Macaulay-matrix endpoints, with AI filling in only the certificate search, or did the AI produce the whole strategy end-to-end?) would settle generated vs. assisted. Expert commentary (a review, Tao-style blog digestion, or journal referee report) on either preprint would allow upgrading status from 'partial' toward 'resolved' for the sub-cases, though the conjecture as a whole would remain open regardless.
